pages.title: What is technical SEO, and how do you do it?

items.question: How does Google find and index web pages?

answers.text: Google's own guide: Google Search works in three stages: crawling, where automated programs download pages they have found; indexing, where Google analyzes a page and stores it in its index; and serving results when someone searches.

Google's own guide: most pages are found automatically, by following links from pages Google already knows or from a sitemap you submit, and Google says it does not guarantee that any page will be crawled, indexed or shown.

items.question: Do I need a sitemap, and what does it do?

answers.text: Google's own guide: a sitemap is a file that tells search engines about the pages, videos and other files on your site and how they relate, so they can crawl the site more efficiently. You might need one if your site is large, new with few links to it, or rich in video and images; you might not if it is small (about 500 pages or fewer) and well linked.
Google's own guide: a sitemap helps search engines discover your URLs, but it does not guarantee that everything listed in it will be crawled and indexed.

items.question: What is robots.txt for, and can it hide a page from Google?

answers.text: Google's own guide: a robots.txt file tells crawlers which URLs on your site they may access, mainly so your site is not overloaded with requests. It is not a way to keep a page out of Google; for that, use noindex or protect the page with a password.
Google's own guide: a page blocked by robots.txt can still be indexed if other sites link to it, and its URL can then appear in results without a description.

items.question: What is a canonical URL, and how do I set one?

answers.text: Google's own guide: when pages are duplicates or very similar, you can tell Google which URL you prefer as the canonical. A redirect or a rel="canonical" link is a strong signal, while listing the URL in your sitemap is a weak one.
Google's own guide: don't use robots.txt or the URL removal tool to choose a canonical, and when you link inside your site, link to the canonical URL rather than a duplicate.

items.question: What are Core Web Vitals?

answers.text: Google's own guide: Core Web Vitals are metrics of real-world user experience: Largest Contentful Paint (loading), Interaction to Next Paint (responsiveness) and Cumulative Layout Shift (visual stability). Google suggests aiming for LCP within 2.5 seconds, INP under 200 milliseconds and CLS under 0.1.

items.question: Does page experience affect Google rankings?

answers.text: Google's own guide: Google's core ranking systems look to reward content with a good page experience; there is no single page experience signal, but Core Web Vitals are used by its ranking systems. Google also says good scores in reports do not guarantee your pages will rank at the top.

items.question: How can I check whether my pages give a good page experience?

answers.text: Google's own guide: ask whether your pages have good Core Web Vitals, are served securely, display well on mobile, avoid excessive ads and intrusive interstitials, and let visitors easily tell the main content from the rest. Google says these questions do not cover every aspect of page experience.

items.question: What is mobile-first indexing, and what should I do about it?

answers.text: Google's own guide: mobile-first indexing means Google uses the mobile version of a site's content, crawled with its smartphone agent, for indexing and ranking. It advises giving the mobile site the same content, headings, structured data, titles and meta descriptions as the desktop site.

Google's own guide: of the three ways to build a mobile-friendly site, Google recommends responsive design, which serves the same HTML on the same URL to every device, because it is the easiest to set up and maintain.

pages.title: What is local SEO, and how do you do it?

items.question: How does Google decide which local businesses to show?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: local results are mainly based on how relevant a business is to the search, how far it is from the searcher, and how well-known it is (prominence); together these help Google find the best match.

items.question: What does relevance mean in local search?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: relevance is how well a Business Profile matches what someone is searching for, and complete, detailed business information helps Google understand your business and match it to relevant searches.

items.question: What do distance and prominence mean in local ranking?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: distance is how far each business is from the person searching, and if they don't share their location, Google uses what it knows about it. Prominence is how well-known a business is, based also on things like how many websites link to it and how many reviews it has.

items.question: Can I pay Google for a better local ranking?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: no; there is no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.

items.question: What information should my Google Business Profile include?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: keep your information complete and accurate, including your full address if customers can visit, your hours (including special hours), what kind of business you are, and details such as parking or Wi-Fi.

items.question: Why should I verify my business on Google?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: verifying tells Google you are authorized to represent the business, which makes it more likely to show up in search results.
Google Business Profile Help: you must verify your business before you can reply to reviews on your Business Profile.

items.question: How should I write my business name on Google?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: use your business's real-world name, as used consistently on your storefront, website and stationery. Adding unnecessary information such as marketing taglines, phone numbers or location details to the name isn't permitted and could lead to suspension.

items.question: How many business categories should I choose?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: use as few categories as possible to describe your core business, pick ones that are specific but representative of your main business, and don't use categories as keywords.

pages.title: What is app store optimization (ASO), and how do you do it?

items.question: How does App Store search decide which apps to show?

answers.text: Apple's own page: App Store search results are based on several factors, including text relevance (matches for your app's title, subtitle, keywords and primary category) and user behavior such as downloads, ratings and reviews.

items.question: How should I choose my app's name on the App Store?

answers.text: Apple's own page: choose a simple, memorable name that is easy to spell and hints at what your app does, and avoid generic terms or names too similar to existing apps. An app name can be up to 30 characters long.

items.question: What is the App Store subtitle for?

answers.text: Apple's own page: the subtitle sums up your app in a short phrase and appears below its name across the App Store; it can be up to 30 characters. Apple suggests highlighting features or typical uses rather than generic lines like "world's best app".

items.question: How do App Store keywords work?

answers.text: Apple's own page: keywords help determine where your app appears in search results, so choose words your audience would use to find an app like yours. They are limited to 100 characters in total, separated by commas with no spaces.
Apple's own page: don't repeat words already in your app name, subtitle or category, and avoid plurals of words you already include, broad terms like "app" or "game", and filler words.

items.question: What should I never put in my App Store keywords?

answers.text: Apple's own page: don't use unauthorized trademarked terms, celebrity names or other protected words, terms not relevant to the app, competing app names, or offensive terms; improper keywords are a common reason for App Store rejections.
Apple's own page: promotional text doesn't affect your app's search ranking, so it should not be used to display keywords.

items.question: How many App Store screenshots can I add, and which ones matter most?

answers.text: Apple's own page: you can feature up to 10 screenshots, and when no app preview is available the first one to three may appear in search results, so they should show the essence of your app.

items.question: What goes into a Google Play store listing?

answers.text: Google Play Console Help: your listing's app details include an app name of up to 30 characters, a short description of up to 80 characters that users see first, and a full description of up to 4,000 characters. Repetitive or irrelevant keywords in these fields can lead to app suspension.

items.question: What is not allowed in a Google Play app title?

answers.text: Google Play Console Help: the title must be 30 characters or less and should not use emojis, emoticons, repeated special characters, or ALL CAPS unless that is your brand. It must not include text that suggests store performance or ranking, price or promotions, or a relation to Google Play programs.

pages.title: How do you show up in Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode?

items.question: What are AI Overviews and AI Mode in Google Search?

answers.text: Google's own guide: AI Overviews help people get the gist of a complicated topic or question quickly, with links to learn more, while AI Mode is meant for questions that need further exploration, reasoning or complex comparisons. Both show links to supporting websites.

items.question: Do I need special optimization to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode?

answers.text: Google's own guide: no; there are no additional requirements or special optimizations to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, and the usual SEO best practices still apply.
answers.card: no additional requirements or special optimizations

items.question: What are the technical requirements to be shown as a link in AI features?

answers.text: Google's own guide: a page must be indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet; there are no additional technical requirements.

Google's own guide: meeting every requirement does not guarantee that Google will crawl, index or serve a page, and AI Overviews often don't appear because they are shown only when Google judges them to add something to classic Search.

items.question: Do I need an AI text file or special schema markup for AI features?

answers.text: Google's own guide: no; you don't need new machine-readable files, AI text files or markup, and there is no special schema.org structured data to add for these features.

items.question: Which SEO basics matter most for AI features?

answers.text: Google's own guide: Google lists making sure crawling is allowed in robots.txt and by your CDN or host, making content easy to find through internal links, a great page experience, important content in text form, and structured data that matches the visible text.
Google's own guide: it also suggests supporting your text with high-quality images and videos where useful, and keeping your Merchant Center and Business Profile information up to date.

items.question: How do I measure traffic from AI Overviews and AI Mode?

answers.text: Google's own guide: sites appearing in AI features are counted in your overall Search Console traffic, in the Performance report under the "Web" search type.
Search Console Help: a click on a link to an external page in an AI Overview counts as a click, and an AI Overview takes one position in the results, which all its links share.

items.question: How can I limit what Google shows from my pages in AI features?

answers.text: Google's own guide: to limit what is shown from your pages in Search, use nosnippet, data-nosnippet, max-snippet or noindex. Robots.txt rules for Googlebot control how your site is crawled for Search, and Google-Extended covers AI training and grounding in some of Google's other systems.

items.question: What is "query fan-out" in Google's AI features?

answers.text: Google's own guide: AI Overviews and AI Mode may use "query fan-out", running several related searches across subtopics and data sources to build a response, which lets them show a wider set of supporting links.

pages.title: How do you get found in ChatGPT and other AI assistants?

items.question: Which crawler does ChatGPT use to find websites for its search answers?

answers.text: OpenAI's own docs: OAI-SearchBot is the crawler used to surface websites in search results in ChatGPT's search features.

items.question: How do I make sure my site can appear in ChatGPT search?

answers.text: OpenAI's own docs: OpenAI recommends allowing OAI-SearchBot in your site's robots.txt file and allowing requests from its published IP ranges.

items.question: Can I block AI training but still appear in ChatGPT search?

answers.text: OpenAI's own docs: yes; the OAI-SearchBot and GPTBot settings are independent, so you can allow OAI-SearchBot to appear in search results while disallowing GPTBot to signal that your content should not be used to train OpenAI's foundation models.

items.question: What happens if I block OAI-SearchBot?

answers.text: OpenAI's own docs: sites that opt out of OAI-SearchBot will not be shown in ChatGPT search answers, though they can still appear as navigational links.

items.question: How long does a robots.txt change take to affect ChatGPT search?

answers.text: OpenAI's own docs: after you update robots.txt, it can take about 24 hours for OpenAI's systems to adjust for search results.

items.question: What is ChatGPT-User, and does robots.txt apply to it?

answers.text: OpenAI's own docs: ChatGPT-User may visit a web page when a user asks ChatGPT or a Custom GPT a question; because these visits are started by a user, robots.txt rules may not apply. It is not used to decide whether content may appear in search, which is managed through OAI-SearchBot.

items.question: How can I see whether Microsoft Copilot cites my pages?

answers.text: Microsoft Bing's own webmaster blog: AI Performance in Bing Webmaster Tools (a public preview) shows how often your content is cited in AI-generated answers across Microsoft Copilot, AI summaries in Bing and some partner integrations, including which URLs are cited and how this changes over time.

items.question: How do I keep my content fresh for Bing and Copilot answers?

answers.text: Microsoft Bing's own webmaster blog: submit a complete XML sitemap with accurate lastmod values, reference it in robots.txt, and use IndexNow to tell Bing when individual URLs are added, updated or removed. Bing also says no tool can guarantee when or how content will appear in AI-generated results.

Microsoft Bing's own webmaster blog: to make content easier for AI systems to reference, Bing suggests clear headings, tables and FAQ sections, supporting claims with evidence, and keeping content up to date.

pages.title: How do reviews help SEO, and how do you manage them?

items.question: Why do Google reviews matter for a business?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: reviews can help your business stand out and give potential customers useful information; they appear next to your Business Profile in Maps and Search.

items.question: Do reviews affect local ranking on Google?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: prominence, one of the main local ranking factors, is partly based on how many reviews a business has, and more reviews and positive ratings can help its local ranking.

items.question: Can I offer customers a discount or gift for a review?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: no; offering incentives such as free or discounted goods or services in exchange for posting, changing or removing reviews counts as fake and misleading content and is strictly prohibited.

items.question: How do I ask customers for Google reviews?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: you can ask customers to leave a review through a Google link or a QR code you create; customers must be signed into a Google Account to leave one.

items.question: How do I reply to a review, and what happens after I reply?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: once your business is verified, open your Business Profile, select Read reviews, then Reply next to the review. Google checks replies against its content policies, and an approved reply is posted publicly and the reviewer is notified.

items.question: How should I reply to a negative review?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: never share a reviewer's private information or attack them personally, be honest about what you can and cannot do, apologize where appropriate, address the reviewer by name, and reply promptly.

items.question: What is a review snippet in Google Search, and when can it appear?

answers.text: Google's own guide: a review snippet is a short excerpt of a review or a rating, often an average of many reviewers' scores; when Google finds valid review or rating markup, it may show a rich snippet with stars.

pages.title: What is image SEO, and how do you do it?

items.question: How does Google find the images on my pages?

answers.text: Google's own guide: use standard HTML image elements; Google can find images in the src attribute of an element, including one inside a element, but it doesn't index CSS images.

items.question: Should I use an image sitemap?

answers.text: Google's own guide: an image sitemap lets you give Google the URLs of images it might not otherwise discover, and unlike regular sitemaps it can include image URLs from other domains, such as a CDN.

items.question: Which image formats does Google Search support?

answers.text: Google's own guide: Google Search supports BMP, GIF, JPEG, PNG, WebP, SVG and AVIF images in the src attribute of , and it suggests making the filename extension match the file type.

items.question: How do I write good alt text for images?

answers.text: Google's own guide: write useful, information-rich alt text that uses keywords appropriately and fits the page's content. Avoid stuffing alt attributes with keywords, which harms the user experience and may make your site look like spam.

items.question: Do image filenames matter for SEO?

answers.text: Google's own guide: filenames give Google very light clues about an image's subject, so use short, descriptive names like my-new-black-kitten.jpg rather than generic ones like IMG00023.JPG.

items.question: How can I choose which image Google shows for my page?

answers.text: Google's own guide: Google picks the preview image automatically, but you can suggest one with schema.org primaryImageOfPage, an image on the page's main entity, or the og:image meta tag. Choose a relevant, high-resolution image, not a generic logo, an image with text, or one with an extreme aspect ratio.

items.question: How should I handle responsive images for Google?

answers.text: Google's own guide: pages can use the <picture> element or the srcset attribute for responsive images, but because some browsers and crawlers don't understand these, always give a fallback URL in the src attribute.

items.question: Can I stop my full-size images from showing in Google Images?

answers.text: Google's own guide: yes; you can opt out of inline linking by checking the HTTP referrer and answering requests from Google domains with a 200 or 204 status and no content. Google will still crawl the page and show a thumbnail made at crawl time.

pages.title: What is video SEO, and how do you do it?

items.question: How does Google find the videos on my pages?

answers.text: Google's own guide: Google can find videos in <video>, <embed>, <iframe> or <object> elements. Don't load the video with URL fragments or require user actions like clicking or swiping, and if JavaScript adds the video, check that it appears in the rendered HTML.

items.question: What does a video need to be indexed by Google?

answers.text: Google's own guide: the watch page must be indexed, the video must be embedded on that page and not hidden behind other elements, and it must have a valid thumbnail at a stable URL. An indexed watch page alone does not mean the video will be indexed.
answers.card: a valid thumbnail at a stable URL

items.question: What is a watch page, and do I need one for each video?

answers.text: Google's own guide: a watch page is a page whose main purpose is to show one video. To be eligible for video features, Google suggests a dedicated watch page for each video where it makes sense, with a title and description unique to that video.

items.question: What are Google's requirements for a video thumbnail?

answers.text: Google's own guide: thumbnails can be BMP, GIF, JPEG, PNG, WebP, SVG or AVIF, at least 60x30 pixels (larger preferred), reachable by Googlebot and not blocked by robots.txt or a login, and available at a stable URL.

items.question: How do I give Google information about my videos?

answers.text: Google's own guide: Google supports video metadata through structured data, video sitemaps and the Open Graph protocol. Keep the structured data consistent with the actual video and give each video a unique thumbnail URL, name and description.

items.question: What are key moments, and how do I enable them?

answers.text: Google's own guide: key moments let users jump between segments of a video like chapters. You can mark them with Clip or SeekToAction structured data, or with timestamps in the YouTube description if the video is on YouTube; Google also tries to detect them automatically.

items.question: How do I make my videos eligible for video previews?

answers.text: Google's own guide: allow Google to fetch your video files so it can pick a few seconds to show as a moving preview; you can cap the preview length with the max-video-preview robots meta tag.

items.question: How do I remove a video from Google Search?

answers.text: Google's own guide: for the fastest removal, file a removal request for the watch page. On your site, return a 404 or add a noindex tag on the watch page, or set an expiration date in structured data or the video sitemap.

pages.title: What is rank tracking, and how do you measure it?

items.question: What does average position mean in Search Console?

answers.text: Search Console Help: average position is the topmost position your link held in Google Search results, averaged across all the queries where your site appeared. For example, topmost positions of 2 and 3 in two queries give an average of 2.5.

items.question: How is a position counted on a Google results page?

answers.text: Search Console Help: positions are usually counted top to bottom on the main side of the page, then on the secondary side, and each result element takes one position even if it holds many links. Ads do not take a search position.

items.question: What counts as an impression?

answers.text: Search Console Help: an impression means a user saw, or may have seen, a link to your site; generally it counts when the link is on the current page of results, even if not scrolled into view. Inside carousels or expanding sections, the item usually has to be scrolled into view or expanded.

items.question: What counts as a click?

answers.text: Search Console Help: for most results, a click is counted when it takes the user to a page outside Google Search, Discover or News. Clicking a result, coming back and clicking the same link again counts as one click.

items.question: How is click-through rate calculated?

answers.text: Search Console Help: click-through rate is clicks divided by impressions.

items.question: Why does Search Console show a different position from what I see when I search?

answers.text: Search Console Help: the reported position is an average over all searches, and your own search can differ because of things like your search history and location.

items.question: How should I read changes in my average position?

answers.text: Search Console Help: position can be misleading, since the same number can mean different places in different layouts. Google recommends watching how position changes over time, especially sudden changes, as well as the absolute value.

items.question: Are AI Overviews counted in Search Console's performance data?

answers.text: Search Console Help: yes; a click on an external link in an AI Overview counts as a click, normal impression rules apply, and all links in the AI Overview share its single position.
Google's own guide: traffic from AI features is included in the Search Console Performance report under the "Web" search type.

pages.title: How do you improve click-through rate with better titles and snippets?

items.question: What is click-through rate (CTR)?

answers.text: Search Console Help: click-through rate is the number of clicks divided by the number of impressions.
answers.card: clicks divided by the number of impressions

items.question: What is a title link in Google Search?

answers.text: Google's own guide: a title link is the title of a search result that links to the page. Google sets it automatically from several sources, but you can show your preferences by following its best practices.

items.question: How do I write a good title for my page?

answers.text: Google's own guide: give every page a <title> element with descriptive, concise text, avoid vague titles like "Home", and avoid repeated or boilerplate titles across pages. There is no length limit, but Google truncates title links as needed, typically to fit the device width.

items.question: Should I repeat my brand name in every title?

answers.text: Google's own guide: your home page title is a reasonable place for extra information about your site, but on other pages consider just adding your site name at the start or end, separated by a hyphen, colon or pipe.

items.question: Why does Google show a different title than the one I wrote?

answers.text: Google's own guide: if Google detects a problem such as a half-empty, outdated or inaccurate title, repeated boilerplate, no clear main heading, or a language mismatch, it may build the title link from other text like headings or anchors.

items.question: What is a snippet, and where does Google get it?

answers.text: Google's own guide: a snippet is the description part of a search result. Google builds it mainly from the page content, and sometimes uses the meta description when it describes the page better.

items.question: How do I write a good meta description?

answers.text: Google's own guide: write a unique description for each page that accurately summarizes it, and include useful details such as author and date for articles or price and manufacturer for products. Avoid long strings of keywords, which are less likely to be shown as a snippet.

items.question: How can I stop or limit snippets for my pages?

answers.text: Google's own guide: use the nosnippet meta tag to prevent a snippet, max-snippet to set a maximum length, and the data-nosnippet attribute to keep certain parts of a page out of snippets.

pages.title: Local SEO checklist: is your Google Business Profile ready?

items.question: Is my business address precise and real?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: use a precise, accurate address or service area for your real-world location. P.O. boxes and mailboxes at remote locations aren't acceptable, and a virtual office you don't operate from isn't eligible.

items.question: If I visit customers instead of having a storefront, should I hide my address?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: yes; a service-area business should hide its address from customers and have one profile for its central office or location with a designated service area.

items.question: Do I have only one profile for my business?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: there should be only one profile per business, and you shouldn't create more than one page for each location, in one account or several.

items.question: Are my business hours set correctly?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: give your regular customer-facing hours, and set special hours for particular days such as holidays or special events.

items.question: Does my business description follow Google's rules?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: use the description for useful information about your services, products, mission and history. It must not contain links of any kind or focus on promotions, prices or sales.

items.question: Is my phone number local and under my control?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: use a local phone number rather than a central call center where possible; the number must be under the business's direct control, and premium numbers are not acceptable.

items.question: Am I asking for reviews and replying to them?

answers.text: Google Business Profile Help: remind customers to leave reviews through a Google link or QR code, and reply to reviews to show customers their feedback matters.
Google Business Profile Help: replying to reviews shows you value customers' feedback, and positive reviews and helpful replies can help your business stand out.

pages.title: App store optimization checklist for the App Store and Google Play

items.question: Have I chosen the most relevant primary category for my app?

answers.text: Apple's own page: your primary and optional secondary category are indexed by App Store search, and choosing categories that aren't relevant is grounds for rejection by App Review.

items.question: Have I localized my App Store product page?

answers.text: Apple's own page: if your app is available in several languages, localize the description, keywords, app previews and screenshots for each market; you can also translate the app's name and tailor keywords to each market.

items.question: Does the first sentence of my App Store description say what makes my app unique?

answers.text: Apple's own page: the first sentence is the most important part of the description because users can read it without tapping to read more, so focus it on your app's unique features. Don't add unnecessary keywords to the description.

items.question: Am I using App Store promotional text the right way?

answers.text: Apple's own page: promotional text appears at the top of the description, is up to 170 characters, and can be updated at any time without a new app version. It doesn't affect search ranking, so don't use it for keywords.

items.question: Am I asking users for ratings in the approved way?

answers.text: Apple's own page: the SKStoreReviewController API lets you prompt users for a rating up to three times in a 365-day period, and you can respond to reviews in App Store Connect. Ratings and reviews influence how your app ranks in search.

items.question: Is my Google Play short description a clear summary?

answers.text: Google Play Console Help: the short description should explain your app's core purpose and biggest benefits in 80 characters or less, be accurate, and leave out offers like "free" or claims like "#1" or "Best".

items.question: Do my Google Play screenshots show the real app experience?

answers.text: Google Play Console Help: use screenshots of the in-app experiences that make your app special, keep text to a minimum, and for screenshots with text provide separate versions for each language you support.

items.question: Is my Google Play description free of keyword lists and anonymous testimonials?

answers.text: Google Play Console Help: don't fill your description with blocks of repeated or unrelated words; describe your app in everyday language. Unattributed or anonymous user testimonials aren't allowed in the description.

AlmiVisibility's own site: no free trial of the plans is named; the site score (3 a day, up to 10 pages) and the title and caption checker are free, with no card.
